author: nicolas
summary: Liraasa 3.0, "Devotion, Music and Measure" (ADR-0021), from the author's 3.0 patch. PROPOSED: PROPOSED: every entry requires the author's ratification before it becomes canon. Additions only: rulings 3.0:G129-G141; the vocative iya; 15 roots and 112 compounds; 17 listed derivations and 1 lexicalised diminutive; 33 restored forms on 2.5 headwords; the clause template, its edges and the miyo, sela and gagu rows follow the rulings. No 2.5 spelling or ruling changes. mernolira, velulira, velurinba, velunulu were already 2.5 words, attested image compounds: each comes back as a headword with its id and takes the patch's meaning, its 2.5 reading archived (for the author's review).

rulings.ruling: iya + noun phrase is a vocative: a direct address. It opens a sentence and is set off by a comma, stands alone as an invocation, or follows a final ki after a comma (2.5:G89). The noun phrase may be a name, a title, an epithet, a pronoun (taivo, taivori) or an owned phrase (maivo de amor). A vocative never changes the grammar of the clause it addresses. In everyday speech a bare name set off by commas remains a vocative (1.2:G31); in prayer, invocation and litany iya is expected, and it is required wherever a comma-set noun phrase could be read as an apposition (3.0:G130).
examples: Iya Deviasa, lenila maivo!
O Great Goddess, hear me!
Iya li mare de li lumi, maivo lirala vobi taivo.
O mother of light, I sing for you.
Taivo viki pagopa ligo maivo ki, iya maivo de amor?
Would you come near me, O my love?
Iya Lumimare!
O Mother of Light!
examples_ungrammatical: iya is not followed by a comma: it belongs to its noun phrase
rulings.notes: The hymn and every prayer genre address the divine; 2.5 had no vocative particle (open question).

rulings.ruling: A noun phrase may be followed by a second noun phrase, set off by commas, that renames it: an apposition. The apposed phrase keeps its own determiner, takes no copula, and is closed by a comma when the clause continues. Each phrase settles its own de-ownership: an apposition starts a new phrase, so it never joins a de-chain (2.5:G96). Several appositions in a row form a litany. A relative clause (raho) may end an apposition.
examples: Li mareasa de li vemiasa, li una-ne lumi raho po kronobioka li veluri, po ke lavisan.
The mother of the cosmos, the first light who gave birth to the stars, was glad.
Deviasa, li mare de li veluri, lirala.
The Great Goddess, the mother of the stars, sings.
li lumi, li lumi de li veluri
the light, the light of the stars
Iya Deviasa, Velumare, Lumimare, Liramare!
O Great Goddess, Mother of the Stars, Mother of Light, Mother of Song!
examples_ungrammatical: Deviasa li mare de li veluri lirala.
an apposition must be set off by commas
rulings.notes: Hymn line 11 (‘The cosmic mother, the first light who birthed stars, was pleased …’) had to be split into two statements; epithets and litanies depend on apposition.

rulings.ruling: An ascended noun or title compound used as a name of the Goddess is capitalized and takes no article (Deviasa, Lumiasa, Mareasa, Velumare). Used as a name, it owns like a personal name when it stands before de (1.2:G27): Deviasa de lira is the Great Goddess’s song. An epithet that describes her keeps its article and stays lower-case: li mare de li lumi, the mother of light. Writing a descriptive epithet as a name therefore changes its meaning.
examples: Deviasa de lira
the Great Goddess’s song (a name owns)
li mareasa de li lumi
the mother of light (an epithet: the light ‘owns’ the relation)
Lumimare lirala.
The Mother of Light sings.
examples_ungrammatical: Mareasa de li lumi (meaning ‘the mother of light’)
as a name, Mareasa owns: this reads ‘the Mother’s light’; write li mareasa de li lumi
rulings.notes: Titles are central to devotion, but 2.5 lets a name before de own; a capitalized ‘Mareasa de li lumi’ would silently mean ‘the Mother’s light’.

rulings.ruling: miyo with a subject before it and no noun phrase after it asserts that the subject exists: absolute being. It takes tense, negation and operators like any verb. miyo + noun phrase with no subject keeps its 2.5 meaning, ‘there is’. A copula (ke, ka) still always needs a predicate.
examples: Saivo miyo.
She is. (She exists.)
Maivo miyo.
I am.
Saivo po miyo, saivo miyo, saivo futu miyo.
She was, she is, she will be.
Kroti li pagoasa, Deviasa po miyo.
Before the universe, the Great Goddess was.
Miyo baba sora en li nimu.
There is a friend in the home. (2.5 meaning, unchanged)
examples_ungrammatical: a copula needs a predicate; use Saivo po miyo
rulings.notes: ‘She was, she is, she will be’ and ‘I am’ could not be said in 2.5; sacred languages need a statement of existence by itself.

rulings.topic: Fiat, blessing of existence, and the liturgical formulas
rulings.ruling: miyo + noun phrase marked as a command (‘!’) is a fiat: ‘let there be …’. miyo + noun phrase + pifu is a wish: ‘may there be …’. Unmarked, miyo + noun phrase stays a statement (2.5:G90). Two fixed liturgical formulas are canon: ‘Ola-modo po miyo, ola-modo miyo, ola-modo futu miyo’ (so it was, so it is, so it shall be), in which ola-modo opens an existential clause without a comma; and ‘Ola-modo pifu’ (so be it; amen), which closes a prayer.
examples: Miyo lumi!
Let there be light!
Miyo sove en li nimu pifu.
May there be peace in the home.
Miyo lumi.
There is light.
Ola-modo po miyo, ola-modo miyo, ola-modo futu miyo.
So it was, so it is, so it shall be.
Ola-modo pifu.
So be it. (Amen.)
examples_ungrammatical: Ola po ka, ola ka, ola futu ka.
rulings.notes: Hymn line 23 had to become ‘that was true, is true, will be true’; creation myths need ‘let there be’.

rulings.ruling: A pronoun or noun phrase + sela in subject position, or as an apposition, is emphatic: ‘herself’, ‘itself’. In object position, PRONOUN sela stays reflexive (unchanged). sela never stands alone as a subject.
examples: Saivo sela po lirala.
She herself sang.
Saivo po amora saivo sela.
She loved herself. (reflexive)
Ito sela po ka li una-ne leninela.
It itself was the first listener.
Saivo de nole po ka sambasan ko li melo, ito sela.
Her name was the same as music, music itself.
examples_ungrammatical: sela needs a pronoun or noun phrase before it
settles_open_questions: sela: reflexive object only, or also emphatic (the maivori half stays open).
rulings.notes: Hymn lines 8 and 17 (‘was itself the first’, ‘music itself’) could not carry the emphasis.

rulings.ruling: A command may carry ne, the iteration words reve and loki, and any adjuncts; it never carries tense, a modal or an evidential. A petition to the divine is a command opened by a vocative (3.0:G129), usually softened by fisa after the vocative’s comma. yava may follow a FRAME.
examples: Iya Deviasa, fisa, ne pagopa vofa maivo!
O Great Goddess, please, do not go far from me!
Reve lirala!
Sing again!
Eli-krono, yava lirala!
Now, let us sing!
Iya Lumimare, fisa, lenila maivo de lirajuba.
O Mother of Light, please hear my song-offering.
settles_open_questions: Which operators a command may carry, and whether yava stands after a FRAME or always first.
rulings.notes: Prayer is built on petitions; 2.5 left open which operators a command may carry and where yava may stand.

rulings.ruling: After a noun naming a made work (lira, lavbulira, lirasarbi, telne, sarbiasa …), gagu + noun phrase names its maker, without a passive verb. Elsewhere gagu remains the agent of gome (2.5:G110).
examples: li lira gagu Peta
the song by Peta
Liraasa, li lira de li una-ne veluri gagu li una-ne mareasa
Liraasa, the song of the first stars, by the first mother
examples_ungrammatical: gagu follows the work, never precedes it
rulings.notes: Hymn line 24 (‘by the first mother’) had to use da, ‘from’.

rulings.ruling: A verbless acclamation NP ala NP! (‘NP to NP!’) is grammatical as a liturgical fragment: glory, praise or thanks offered to someone. It may be followed by a vocative.
examples: Lumisirmo ala Deviasa!
Glory to the Great Goddess!
Benaseno ala taivo, iya Lumimare!
Praise to you, O Mother of Light!
Lorejuba ala taivo, iya Velumare.
Thanks to you, O Mother of the Stars.
rulings.notes: Doxologies and praise lines (‘Glory to …’) had no form.

rulings.ruling: Taivo, Saivo and their forms may be capitalized mid-sentence when they refer to the Goddess. This is an optional convention of written devotion and has no grammatical effect.
examples: Maivo amora Taivo.
I love You.
Saivo miyo, ata Saivo de lumi lumila.
She is, and Her light shines.

rulings.ruling: The new noun rinbakrono (eternity) is a time noun: as ‘when’ it takes en (2.5:G103). en rinbakrono means ‘for ever; in eternity’. toda-krono (always) is unchanged. Durations in general (‘for two days’) remain an open question.
examples: Saivo futu lirala en rinbakrono.
She will sing for ever.
Maivo amora taivo toda-krono.
I love you always.

rulings.ruling: A bare noun or number repeated around krotiapo (‘X after X’) is a distributive adjunct or FRAME meaning ‘one X after another’: una krotiapo una, one by one; velu krotiapo velu, star after star. It extends kroti/krotiapo + a bare noun (2.3:G79).
examples: Una krotiapo una, li veluri po hiro lirala.
One by one, the stars began to sing.
Velu krotiapo velu, li navu po loya lumisan.
Star after star, the sky became bright.
rulings.notes: Hymn line 12 (‘One by one, star by star’) had no form.

rulings.ruling: Ascended forms are most powerful against ordinary ones. Keep ordinary forms for the human and the near; reserve ascended forms for what is truly divine; let a change of register mark a change of nearness (a mortal growing toward the divine, or the Goddess stooping to comfort). This is guidance for composition, not grammar.
examples: Maivo ke nemesan. Taivo ka loreasa.
I am sorrowful. You are a heart larger than sorrow.
